Hi Mark. Last class you told the story of a trip through what was done. Today you talk to the people on that trip. When you meet somebody on a train, a direct question like have you been to Osaka is correct, but it sounds like a form. A question tag sounds like a conversation. You say what you think is true, and you add a tiny question. You've been to Osaka, haven't you? The rule is simple. Copy the auxiliary from the sentence, and turn it around. A positive sentence gets a negative tag, and a negative sentence gets a positive one. You didn't take the fast train, did you? If there is no auxiliary, use do, does or did. She likes sushi, doesn't she? There are a few special ones. I'm late becomes aren't I. Let's go becomes shall we. And an instruction becomes will you. Now the traps. In Portuguese, one little word works for everything, and many Brazilians use isn't it for every sentence. It only works after it is. Second, never and nobody are already negative, so the tag is positive. Nobody told you, did they? And third, listen to your voice. If it goes down, you are sure. If it goes up, it is a real question. Before class, write ten sentences about the trip, each with a tag.

Okay, everybody, welcome to Kamo River Hostel. You all found us without any problems, didn't you? Good. I'm Kenji, and this kitchen is the heart of the house, so you'll spend a lot of time here, won't you? Let me explain a few things. Breakfast isn't included, but there's plenty of rice and tea, and nobody will charge you for that, will they? You've all taken your shoes off, haven't you? Great. Now, most of you have never been to Kyoto before, have you? Then here is my one piece of advice. Talk to each other. Half of the best stories I hear started in this kitchen, with somebody saying something like, you're from Brazil, aren't you? Tonight a few of us are going to the night market by the river. You can tag along if you want. It's not far, and it's free. Let's meet here at seven, shall we? Oh, and one last thing. Keep your voices down after eleven, will you? The walls are thin. Enjoy your stay.

Excuse me, this train goes to Osaka, doesn't it? It does. You're not from here, are you? No, I'm from Brazil. You've been to Osaka before, haven't you? Many times. My cousin lives there. I could show you around the market, if you like. That would be great. Let's meet at the station at ten, shall we?
